text:
Some coding rounds now come with an assistant built in, so the code will get written either way. What's graded is everything around it: what you ask for, what you accept, and what you check. Seven questions: three on the round itself, three on designing features that call a large language model, or LLM, and one behavioral question that's become common.

Question one. In an AI-allowed round, what are interviewers actually grading? Not whether working code exists at the end. Whether you drove. Canva's write-up of its first AI-assisted interviews said the strong candidates didn't just prompt AI and accept whatever it generated. The ones who struggled lacked the judgment to steer the tool, not the ability to code. Google's pilot rubric names the same three skills: writing prompts, validating the output, and debugging. What scores well: you plan before you prompt, restating the requirement and sketching an approach yourself. You break the work into small, well-specified requests. You read every line it writes, like a colleague's pull request. You run it, test it and probe the edges. And when it's wrong, you say so. The red flags: accepting code you can't explain, letting the assistant choose the design, long silences while it generates, and prompting for things that would be faster to type. One prep guide's advice is worth keeping: better to solve part of the problem by hand than to present a solution you can't explain.
